conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes 'Yes' and presents evidence from the pivotal FREEDOM trial showing a statistically significant 68% relative risk reduction in new vertebral fractures for patients treated with denosumab compared to placebo.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
**Conclusion: Yes.** Denosumab (Prolia) substantially reduces *new radiographic (morphometric) vertebral fractures* in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis.

The strongest evidence is the pivotal randomized, placebo-controlled FREEDOM trial. At 36 months, new vertebral fractures occurred in **2.3%** of women assigned denosumab (86/3,702) versus **7.2%** assigned placebo (264/3,691). This was a **68% relative risk reduction** (risk ratio 0.32; 95% CI 0.26–0.41; *P*<0.001). The **absolute reduction was 4.9 percentage points**—roughly one vertebral fracture prevented for every 20 women treated for three years, based on these trial results.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa0809493

The FDA-approved Prolia label independently reports that reductions in new morphometric vertebral fractures were statistically significant at years 1, 2, and 3, with the same year-3 incidence (2.3% vs 7.2%; *P*<0.0001).  
https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2025/125320Orig1s221lbl.pdf

**Important interpretation:** this evidence directly applies chiefly to the studied population—postmenopausal women with osteoporosis—and the endpoint includes X-ray-detected fractures, not only painful symptomatic fractures. The benefit also depends on continued, appropriately managed treatment: the FDA label warns that vertebral fractures, sometimes multiple, have occurred after stopping Prolia, as early as seven months after the last dose; prior vertebral fracture predicts higher risk.  
https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2024/125320s216lbl.pdf
